name: Firebolt
license: Proprietary. Firebolt Core, the free self-hosted engine, ships as binaries only under the Elastic License 2.0 (source-available terms, not OSI open source; a custom licence before July 2025). SDKs, dbt adapter and Kubernetes operator are Apache 2.0
summary: A cloud data warehouse built for low-latency, high-concurrency queries behind apps and dashboards, also free to self-host as Firebolt Core.
intro: Firebolt keeps table data in object storage (S3 in the managed service) as immutable files called tablets, each sorted on the table’s `PRIMARY INDEX`. A sparse index with one entry per granule of 8,192 rows lets a scan binary-search to the few granules that can match, and every compute node caches the tablets it reads on local SSD. Compute comes as engines: an engine is one or more clusters of S, M, L or XL nodes, and any engine can query any database, so loading and serving can run on separate engines over the same data. Two features target the latency of repeated, app-style queries: aggregating indexes, which precompute a `GROUP BY` and are updated in the same transaction as the base table, and caching of subresults such as join hash tables across queries. The SQL dialect follows PostgreSQL, and the engine also reads Iceberg tables in place.

The managed service runs in six AWS regions and bills engines per second in Firebolt Units (FBUs): a storage-optimized S node is 8 FBUs an hour, and compute-optimized nodes, with smaller SSD caches, are half that. On the Standard edition an FBU costs $0.23 an hour in US regions, so an S node is $1.84 an hour; Enterprise adds multi-cluster auto-scaling, PrivateLink and HIPAA at $0.35 per FBU. Storage is passed through at S3 cost, $27.07 per TiB-month in US East. Firebolt Core, launched in June 2025, is the same query engine as a free Docker image for laptops or your own clusters, under the Elastic License 2.0, which forbids offering it as a hosted service. In 2026 Firebolt’s site describes the engine as open source “in preview”, but the source repository its build guide points to is not public.
strengths: Built for many concurrent, repetitive queries: aggregating indexes stay consistent with every write, and subresult caching reuses work across queries
Engines scale up (node type), out (nodes) and for concurrency (clusters) online, and several engines can share one copy of the data
PostgreSQL-compliant SQL, including its error behaviour, rather than a vendor dialect
The same engine runs free on a laptop or your own hardware as Firebolt Core, with no usage limits
Reads Iceberg tables in place and can mount whole catalogs (REST, Glue, Unity, Snowflake Open Catalog) as databases
limits: Not open source today: Core is a closed binary under the Elastic License 2.0, and the announced open-source release was still a preview with a waitlist in October 2026
Engines bill while running, and `AUTO_STOP` defaults to 20 minutes of idle time; L and XL nodes need a request to support
Deleted data keeps costing storage for a fixed 7-day recovery window that can’t be changed
The managed service is AWS only, in six regions; multi-cluster auto-scaling and PrivateLink need the Enterprise edition at about 50% more per FBU
Fast queries depend on choosing primary and aggregating indexes well; a filter on a transformed column or outside the index keys reads much more data

notes: An engine costs node price × nodes × clusters. Enterprise is $0.35 per FBU in the US; outside the US, Standard is $0.28 and Enterprise $0.42. Committed-use discounts go through sales.
The pricing calculator lists a compute-optimized S node with 8 vCPU, 16 GB of RAM and a 475 GB SSD cache.
Storage is $27.07 per TiB-month in US East, US West and Ireland, $28.84 in Frankfurt and $29.43 in Singapore and Mumbai. New accounts get $200 in credits.

items.name: Managed service
items.text: Firebolt runs engines and storage in its AWS account in six regions. Dedicated adds single-tenant infrastructure; its price is by quote.

items.name: Firebolt Core
items.text: The same query engine as a multi-arch Docker image, from one laptop to a multi-node cluster. Needs Linux 6.1 or newer for `io_uring`; queries go over HTTP on port 3473. Can’t be resold as a hosted service.

items.name: Kubernetes operator
items.text: Apache 2.0 operator and Helm chart that run engines, a metadata service backed by PostgreSQL and a gateway in your own cluster, over S3, GCS or Azure Blob Storage.

story: Eldad Farkash, Saar Bitner and Ariel Yaroshevich had built the BI company Sisense, where cloud data warehouses struggled with terabytes of data behind interactive dashboards. They founded Firebolt in 2019 to make warehouse queries fast and cheap enough for user-facing workloads, and came out of stealth in December 2020 with $37 million.

Writing a warehouse from scratch would have taken years, so the team assembled one and had production customers in under 18 months. The runtime was a hard fork of ClickHouse, chosen for its vectorised speed and basic scale-out. The SQL parser and planner started from Hyrise, an academic database from HPI, because it was also C++ and simple to extend, and the logical plan was redesigned along the lines of Apache Calcite. Firebolt then replaced ClickHouse’s distributed execution with its own shuffle-based stages and rewrote most functions to behave like PostgreSQL.

A $100 million Series C in January 2022 valued the company at $1.4 billion, and Mosha Pasumansky joined from Google BigQuery as CTO. In June 2025 Firebolt released Firebolt Core, the engine as a free download, and said it kept it closed so it couldn’t easily be copied; its licence became the Elastic License 2.0 that July.

choices.choice: Fork the ClickHouse runtime instead of writing one
choices.why: ClickHouse was fast, battle-tested and already did basic distributed queries, which let a small startup ship quickly. A hard fork left Firebolt free to change interfaces and replace whole layers later.

choices.choice: Planner and runtime in the same language
choices.why: Much database work happens where planner and runtime meet. With a C++ runtime, a C++ planner (from Hyrise rather than Java-based Calcite) let engineers work across both without switching stacks.
PostgreSQL is widely known, close to ANSI SQL and raises errors early, for example on overflow. Matching it meant overhauling scalar and aggregate functions without giving up vectorised speed.

choices.choice: Maintain aggregating indexes in the same transaction
choices.why: Apps run the same aggregations constantly. Updating precomputed groups incrementally on every write moves work from reads to writes, so reads after a commit never hit a stale or recomputing index.
